citation.title: A Note on Dropping Experimental Subjects who Fail a Manipulation Check

standing_assumptions: [Setting: Section 2, p. 573 (PDF p. 2)] “Suppose we have an i.i.d. sample from $(Y, S, Z)$, where $Y$ denotes the subject's response, $S$ denotes the result of a manipulation check (1 if the subject passed, 0 if the subject failed), and $Z$ denotes the subject's treatment assignment (1 for treatment 1, 2 for treatment 2, . . .). Without loss of generality, assume that the support of $Z$ is $\{1, \ldots, K\}$, where $K$ is finite. We make three assumptions to proceed. First, we assume that both potential responses and potential results from the manipulation check are stable, by invoking SUTVA (Rubin 1980), which implies both no interference between units and no multiple unobserved versions of the treatment.” [p. 573] ASSUMPTION 1 (SUTVA). $Y = \sum_{z=1}^{K} Y(z)\mathbf{I}(Z = z)$ and $S = \sum_{z=1}^{K} S(z)\mathbf{I}(Z = z)$. [p. 573] “Second, we assume that the treatment is not systematically related to potential outcomes or potential manipulation check results, as would be ensured by random assignment of the treatment.” [p. 574 (PDF p. 3)] ASSUMPTION 2 (Ignorability). For all $z \in \{1, \ldots, K\}$, $(Y(z), S(z)) \perp\!\!\!\perp Z$, with $\Pr(Z = z) > 0$. “Assumption 2 can be ensured at the design stage by randomizing treatment assignment across subjects.” [p. 574] “Finally, we require that at least some subjects pass the manipulation check in both treatment and control.” ASSUMPTION 3 (Nonzero Passing Rates). For all $z \in \{1, \ldots, K\}$, $\Pr[S|Z = z] > 0$. “Note that Assumption 3 is verifiable from the experimental data.” [As printed the event is missing; $\Pr[S = 1|Z = z] > 0$ is meant (finding P010-N002, corrected in P010-T17). Every target uses the corrected form.] [Regularity: Section 2.1, p. 574] “As we proceed, plug-in estimators will be consistent given suitable regularity conditions (e.g., finite third moments, continuity), with the bootstrap providing a basis for asymptotic inference.” [The paper puts no moment condition inside its numbered results. Each conditional mean written in a target is taken to exist; finite first moments of $Y(1), \ldots, Y(K)$ ensure this.] [Target parameter: Section 2.1, p. 574] “Here we consider one possible target that seems natural: $\mathrm{E}[Y(z) - Y(z')|S(1) = S(2) = \cdots = S(K) = 1]$, or the average treatment effect among subjects who would pass under all treatment conditions.” [Covariates: Section 2.3, p. 576 (PDF p. 5)] “Suppose that we had a vector of covariates $\mathbf{X}$ associated with each unit, so that we now have an i.i.d. sample from $(Y, S, Z, \mathbf{X})$. We can now write an assumption analogous to Assumption 2.” ASSUMPTION 4 (Ignorability with Covariates). For all $z \in \{1, \ldots, K\}$, $(Y(z), S(z), \mathbf{X}) \perp\!\!\!\perp Z$, with $\Pr(Z = z) > 0$. [Notation] $Y(z)$ and $S(z)$ are the potential response and the potential result of the manipulation check under treatment $z$; the paper introduces them only through Assumption 1. $\mathrm{E}$ and $\Pr$ refer to the joint law of one draw $(Y(1), \ldots, Y(K), S(1), \ldots, S(K), Z)$ (with $\mathbf{X}$ in Section 2.3), of which $(Y, S, Z)$ is the observed part. $\perp\!\!\!\perp$ is independence, and $\mathbf{X} \perp\!\!\!\perp Z|S$ is conditional independence given $S$. $z$ and $z'$ range over $\{1, \ldots, K\}$. Every numbered result is a statement about this population law; no target is asymptotic. The paper does not define ‘sharp bounds’. The targets use the usual meaning: the infimum and supremum of the target parameter over all joint laws of the potential variables and $Z$ that satisfy the assumptions and induce the given law of the observables $(Y, S, Z)$.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Footnote 7, the weight $\frac{p_i}{1-p_i}$ with $R_i = 1$ for the replication study, as printed
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed statement refuted: footnote 7, p. 578 (PDF p. 7)] “Let $R_i = 1$ if an observation $i$ is in the replication study, else let $R_i = 0$ if an observation was in the original data. We performed a logistic regression of $R_i$ on the following covariates $\mathbf{X}_i$: Education, Party, Religion, Political Interest, Income, Gender, News Interest, Voter Registration, Birth Year, Region, Race, and Ideology (with mean-imputation for missingness). Using the output of this logistic regression, we computed a predicted value $p_i = \Pr[R_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i]$ for each observation $i$. To reweight the replication study to the original study's covariate profile, we weighted each observation in the replication sample by $\frac{p_i}{1-p_i}$.” [Formal reading] With $R = 1$ for the replication study and $p(x) = \Pr[R = 1|X = x]$, weighting the replication observations by $w(x) = p(x)/(1 - p(x))$ reproduces the original study's covariate distribution: $f_R(x)w(x)/\sum_u f_R(u)w(u) = f_O(x)$ for every $x$. [Counterexample, from the validator] Eight subjects and one binary covariate. The four original subjects ($R = 0$) have $X = (0, 0, 0, 1)$ and the four replication subjects ($R = 1$) have $X = (0, 1, 1, 1)$, so $f_O = (3/4, 1/4)$ and $f_R = (1/4, 3/4)$ on $\{0, 1\}$. The logistic regression of $R$ on $X$ with an intercept is saturated; its unique maximum-likelihood fit is $p(0) = 1/4$, $p(1) = 3/4$ (intercept $\log(1/3)$, slope $\log 9$), which are the true conditional probabilities. The printed weights are $p/(1 - p) = 1/3$ at $x = 0$ and $3$ at $x = 1$; the weighted replication masses are $(1/4)(1/3) = 1/12$ and $(3/4)(3) = 9/4$, with sum $7/3$, so the weighted replication share of $X = 1$ is $27/28$, not the original study's $1/4$. The reciprocal weights $(1 - p)/p = 3$ and $1/3$ give masses $3/4$ and $1/4$, which is exactly $f_O$.

We performed a logistic regression of $R_i$ on the following covariates $\mathbf{X}_i$: Education, Party, Religion, Political Interest, Income, Gender, News Interest, Voter Registration, Birth Year, Region, Race, and Ideology (with mean-imputation for missingness). Using the output of this logistic regression, we computed a predicted value $p_i = \Pr[R_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i]$ for each observation $i$. To reweight the replication study to the original study's covariate profile, we weighted each observation in the replication sample by $\frac{p_i}{1-p_i}$.” [Sentence carrying the footnote, Section 3, p. 578] “For our primary analysis, we used inverse probability weighting (IPW) to adjust the replication sample to match the covariate distribution of the sample used in PSV, and computed estimates after weighting.” [Notation of the targets, not in the paper: $f_O$ and $f_R$ are the covariate distributions of the original and the replication sample, $\pi = \Pr(R = 1)$ the share of the pooled data from the study coded 1.]
canonical_claim.note: P010-E007 is rated an error, Minor: the footnote's stated coding reverses the odds, while the deposited code codes the original (PSV) rows as 1 and weights replication rows by the odds of original membership, which is the intended direction; no number changes. The example has overlap, a finite maximum-likelihood fit and no misspecification, so it isolates the direction of the odds. The validator's check.py verifies it with exact fractions.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Footnote 7, corrected (coding of the study indicator, or equivalently the direction of the odds)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Corrected footnote 7, from Sol's smallest repair: only the first sentence changes] “Let $R_i = 1$ if observation $i$ is in the original study, and let $R_i = 0$ if it is in the replication study.” The rest is unchanged: $p_i = \Pr[R_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i]$, and each observation in the replication sample is weighted by $ rac{p_i}{1-p_i}$. Equivalently, keeping the printed coding ($R_i = 1$ for the replication study), the weight is $ rac{1-p_i}{p_i}$. [Formal content] Let $R \in \{0, 1\}$ with $R = 1$ for the replication study, $\pi = \Pr(R = 1) \in (0, 1)$, $p(x) = \Pr(R = 1|X = x)$, and let $f_R$ and $f_O$ be probability mass functions, or probability densities with respect to a common dominating measure $
u$, of $X$ given $R=1$ and given $R=0$, respectively, positive on their common support, on which $0<p(x)<1$. Then: (i) $ rac{p(x)}{1 - p(x)} =  rac{\pi}{1 - \pi} rac{f_R(x)}{f_O(x)}$, so $ rac{f_O(x)}{f_R(x)} =  rac{\pi}{1 - \pi} rac{1 - p(x)}{p(x)}$; (ii) with $w(x) = (1 - p(x))/p(x)$, $f_R(x)w(x)/\sum_u f_R(u)w(u) = f_O(x)$ on the common support (almost everywhere in the density formulation): the replication sample weighted by the odds of membership in the original study has the original study's covariate distribution, and a constant factor in the weights cancels; (iii) with the printed weight $w(x)=p(x)/(1-p(x))$, suppose additionally that $Z=\sum_u f_R(u)^2/f_O(u)<\infty$ (or $Z=\int f_R(u)^2/f_O(u)\,d
u(u)<\infty$ in the density formulation). Then $Z>0$ and the normalized weighted mass function or density is $\{f_R(x)^2/f_O(x)\}/Z$, which equals $f_O$ only if $f_R=f_O$ (almost everywhere in the density formulation). If $Z=\infty$, these printed weights have infinite total mass and do not define a probability distribution by normalization. (Sums are over the support of a discrete covariate; integrals with respect to $
u$ replace them for densities. This extra finite-normalizer condition is only for (iii); the corrected-odds normalizer in (ii) is automatically $(1-\pi)/\pi$.)
canonical_claim.definitions_needed:
[Footnote 7, p. 578 (PDF p. 7), in full] “Let $R_i = 1$ if an observation $i$ is in the replication study, else let $R_i = 0$ if an observation was in the original data. We performed a logistic regression of $R_i$ on the following covariates $\mathbf{X}_i$: Education, Party, Religion, Political Interest, Income, Gender, News Interest, Voter Registration, Birth Year, Region, Race, and Ideology (with mean-imputation for missingness). Using the output of this logistic regression, we computed a predicted value $p_i = \Pr[R_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i]$ for each observation $i$. To reweight the replication study to the original study's covariate profile, we weighted each observation in the replication sample by $ rac{p_i}{1-p_i}$.” [Sentence carrying the footnote, Section 3, p. 578] “For our primary analysis, we used inverse probability weighting (IPW) to adjust the replication sample to match the covariate distribution of the sample used in PSV, and computed estimates after weighting.” [Notation of the targets, not in the paper: $f_O$ and $f_R$ are the covariate distributions of the original and the replication sample, $\pi = \Pr(R = 1)$ the share of the pooled data from the study coded 1.] In the density formulation, $f_R$ and $f_O$ are measurable positive $
u$-almost-everywhere probability densities on the shared support, with unit integrals, and the Bayes and density equalities are understood $
u$-almost everywhere. For (iii) only, $Z=\int f_R^2/f_O\,d
u$ must be finite; in the discrete formulation the same condition is $Z=\sum_x f_R(x)^2/f_O(x)<\infty$. The true propensity is the version $p(x)=\pi f_R(x)/\{\pi f_R(x)+(1-\pi)f_O(x)\}$ on that support. These exact population identities make no claim of exact balance for a fitted logistic propensity.
canonical_claim.note: Both forms of the repair are given by Sol and judged equivalent; reversing the indicator definition is the one that matches the deposited code (abp_replication.R: PSV rows have dataset = 1, replication rows dataset = 0, and replication rows get probs/(1 - probs)). Repair cost: none. The formal content is Section 2 of the validator's derivation; it uses true conditional probabilities and makes no claim that a fitted logistic model balances the covariates exactly.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Appendix A, proof of Proposition 1, the display ‘a sharp upper bound is given by $\mathrm{E}[Y(1)|U = 1, S(1) = 1] \le \mathrm{E}[Y(1)|Y(1) \le Q_{Y(1)|S(1)=1}(1 - \ldots)]$’, as printed
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed statement refuted: Appendix A, proof of Proposition 1, p. 580 (PDF p. 9), with $U = 1$ if $S(2) = \cdots = S(K) = 1$ and $U = 0$ otherwise] “Thus if $\frac{\sum_{k=2}^{K}\Pr[S(k)=0]}{\Pr[S(1)=1]} < 1$, a sharp upper bound is given by $\mathrm{E}[Y(1)|U = 1, S(1) = 1] \le \mathrm{E}[Y(1)|Y(1) \le Q_{Y(1)|S(1)=1}(1 - \sum_{k=2}^{K}\frac{\Pr[S(k)=0]}{\Pr[S(1)=1]})]$, else the upper bound is infinite.” [Counterexample, from the validator] $K = 2$. $B \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(4/5)$, $Y(1) \sim N(0, 1)$ and $Z$ uniform on $\{1, 2\}$ are mutually independent; $S(1) = S(2) = B$; $Y(2) = Y(1)$ (the validator leaves $Y(2)$ unspecified; it plays no part); $Y = Y(Z)$, $S = S(Z)$. Then Assumptions 1–3 hold, $\Pr[S(1) = S(2) = 1] = 4/5 > 0$, $Y$ is continuous with unbounded support, and $U = B$. The ratio is $\Pr[S(2) = 0]/\Pr[S(1) = 1] = (1/5)/(4/5) = 1/4 < 1$. The left-hand side is $\mathrm{E}[Y(1)|U = 1, S(1) = 1] = \mathrm{E}[Y(1)|B = 1] = 0$. The printed right-hand side is $\mathrm{E}[Y(1)|Y(1) \le Q_{Y(1)|S(1)=1}(3/4)] = \mathrm{E}[Y(1)|Y(1) \le \Phi^{-1}(3/4)] = -\varphi(\Phi^{-1}(3/4))/(3/4) \approx -0.4237020969 < 0$. The printed inequality asserts $0 \le -0.4237020969$ and is false. (The corrected right-hand side of P010-T14 is $\mathrm{E}[Y(1)|Y(1) \ge \Phi^{-1}(1/4), S(1) = 1] = \varphi(\Phi^{-1}(1/4))/(3/4) \approx 0.4237020969$.)
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [Appendix A, proof of Proposition 1, p. 580 (PDF p. 9), up to the display at issue] “Proof of Proposition 1. We will follow the general logic of Lee (2009), and technical details carry through from the proof of Lee's Proposition 1a. Without loss of generality, we consider the upper bound for $\mathrm{E}[Y(1)|S(1) = S(2) = \cdots = S(K) = 1]$. Define $U = 1$ if $S(2) = \cdots = S(K) = 1$, else let $U = 0$. Then $\mathrm{E}[Y(1)|S(1) = S(2) = \cdots = S(K) = 1] = \mathrm{E}[Y(1)|U = 1, S(1) = 1]$. We do not observe the joint distribution of $(Y(1), U)|S(1) = 1$, as we never jointly observe $Y(z)$ and $S(z')$, for $z \ne z'$. Let $p_{U^0} = \Pr[U = 0|S(1) = 1]$. Given continuity of $Y(1)$, then among all possible joint distributions $(Y(1), U)|S(1) = 1$, $\mathrm{E}[Y(1)|U = 1, S(1) = 1]$ is maximized when $U = 1$ for all $Y(1) \ge Q_{Y(1)}(p_{U^0})$. By weak monotonicity of the quantile function, it suffices to maximize $p_{U^0}$ to find a maximum for $\mathrm{E}[Y(1)|U = 1, S(1) = 1]$. We again do not observe the joint distribution $(U, S(1))$. By $\sigma$-additivity, a sharp upper bound is obtained for $\Pr[U = 0]$ is obtained when the regions where $S(2), S(3), \ldots, S(K)$ each equal zero are disjoint, with $$\Pr[U = 0] \le \begin{cases} \sum_{k=2}^{K} \Pr[S(k) = 0] & : \sum_{k=2}^{K} \Pr[S(k) = 0] < 1 \\ 1 & : \sum_{k=2}^{K} \Pr[S(k) = 0] \ge 1. \end{cases}$$ Thus, among all possible joint distributions $(U, S(1))$, $\Pr[U = 0|S(1) = 1] = p_{U^0}$ is maximized when $$p_{U^0} = \begin{cases} \frac{\sum_{k=2}^{K} \Pr[S(k) = 0]}{\Pr[S(1) = 1]} & : \frac{\sum_{k=2}^{K} \Pr[S(k) = 0]}{\Pr[S(1) = 1]} < 1 \\ 1 & : \frac{\sum_{k=2}^{K} \Pr[S(k) = 0]}{\Pr[S(1) = 1]} \ge 1. \end{cases}$$” [$Q_{Y(1)|S(1)=1}$ is used in the proof without a separate definition: the quantile function of the conditional distribution of $Y(1)$ given $S(1) = 1$. Proposition 1 itself is transcribed in P010-T3.]
canonical_claim.note: P010-E004 is rated an error, Minor: a misprint in one proof display (the lower tail written for the upper bound); the sentence before it, the next display and the Proposition have the upper tail. The qualitative fact behind the example is that the mean of the lower three quarters of a centred normal distribution is strictly negative; the decimal is from the validator's checks.py (scipy), not from exact arithmetic. Because $Y(1)$ is independent of $B$ here, the missing conditioning on $S(1) = 1$ in the printed right-hand side does not affect the value.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Appendix A, proof of Proposition 1, first upper-bound display, corrected
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed, p. 580 (PDF p. 9)] “Given continuity of $Y(1)$, then among all possible joint distributions $(Y(1), U)|S(1) = 1$, $\mathrm{E}[Y(1)|U = 1, S(1) = 1]$ is maximized when $U = 1$ for all $Y(1) \ge Q_{Y(1)}(p_{U^0})$.” [...] “Thus if $\frac{\sum_{k=2}^{K}\Pr[S(k)=0]}{\Pr[S(1)=1]} < 1$, a sharp upper bound is given by $\mathrm{E}[Y(1)|U = 1, S(1) = 1] \le \mathrm{E}[Y(1)|Y(1) \le Q_{Y(1)|S(1)=1}(1 - \sum_{k=2}^{K}\frac{\Pr[S(k)=0]}{\Pr[S(1)=1]})]$, else the upper bound is infinite.” [Corrected, from Sol's smallest repair. Changes: the lower-tail event $Y(1) \le Q(1 - r)$ becomes the upper-tail event $Y(1) \ge Q(r)$; $S(1) = 1$ is added to the conditioning event of the tail mean; in the earlier sentence $Q_{Y(1)}(p_{U^0})$ becomes $Q_{Y(1)|S(1)=1}(p_{U^0})$.] With $r = \sum_{k=2}^{K}\Pr[S(k) = 0]/\Pr[S(1) = 1] < 1$, $$\mathrm{E}[Y(1)|U = 1, S(1) = 1] \le \mathrm{E}[Y(1)|Y(1) \ge Q_{Y(1)|S(1)=1}(r), S(1) = 1].$$ [Corrected statement in full] Let $U = 1$ if $S(2) = \cdots = S(K) = 1$ and $U = 0$ otherwise, and suppose that $\Pr[S(1) = S(2) = \cdots = S(K) = 1] > 0$ and that the conditional distribution of $Y(1)$ given $S(1) = 1$ is continuous with finite mean. Then: (i) for any value $p \in [0, 1)$ of $p_{U^0} = \Pr[U = 0|S(1) = 1]$, among all joint distributions of $(Y(1), U)$ given $S(1) = 1$ with that value, $\mathrm{E}[Y(1)|U = 1, S(1) = 1]$ is maximized when $U = 1$ exactly for $Y(1) \ge Q_{Y(1)|S(1)=1}(p)$, and the maximum $\mathrm{E}[Y(1)|Y(1) \ge Q_{Y(1)|S(1)=1}(p), S(1) = 1]$ is nondecreasing in $p$; (ii) $p_{U^0} \le r$, with $r = \sum_{k=2}^{K}\Pr[S(k) = 0]/\Pr[S(1) = 1]$; (iii) if $r < 1$, then $\mathrm{E}[Y(1)|U = 1, S(1) = 1] \le \mathrm{E}[Y(1)|Y(1) \ge Q_{Y(1)|S(1)=1}(r), S(1) = 1]$.

canonical_claim.note: The prior correction (use the upper-tail event $Y(1) \ge Q_1(t)$ in place of $Y(1) \le Q_1(1 - t)$) was judged correct with changes: add $S(1) = 1$ to the tail expectation and the conditional subscript to the earlier quantile. Parts (i)–(iii) are the content of the proof's own argument (‘By weak monotonicity of the quantile function, it suffices to maximize $p_{U^0}$’) and of the validator's derivation; they involve the potential variables only, and the translation to observables is P010-T15. The clause ‘else the upper bound is infinite’ is the subject of P010-E002 (P010-T6). The sharpness wording of this paragraph of the proof (disjoint failure regions; the value one as a maximum) is a clarity note (P010-E006) and has no target.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Appendix A, proof of Proposition 1, final upper-bound display, corrected
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed, p. 580 (PDF p. 9)] “By random assignment and SUTVA, the conditional distribution of $Y(1)|S(1) = 1$ is equivalent to the conditional distribution of $Y|S = 1, Z = 1$, and the marginal distributions of $S(k)$ are each equivalent to $S|Z = k$. Thus a sharp upper bound is given by $\mathrm{E}[Y(1)|U = 1, S(1) = 1] \le \mathrm{E}[Y|Y \ge Q_{Y|Z=1,S=1}(\sum_{k=2}^{K} \frac{\Pr[S=0|Z=k]}{\Pr[S=1|Z=k]}), Z = 1]$ when $\sum_{k=2}^{K} \frac{\Pr[S=0|Z=k]}{\Pr[S=1|Z=k]} < 1$, else the upper bound is infinite. The bounds are invariant to indexing of treatments $Z$, thus yielding the general upper bound in Proposition 1. Analogous calculations yield lower bounds.” [Corrected display, from Sol's smallest repair. Changes: both denominators $\Pr[S = 1|Z = k]$ become $\Pr[S = 1|Z = 1]$, the passing rate of the arm being bounded; $S = 1$ is added to the outer conditioning event (finding P010-E001).] With $r_1 = \sum_{k=2}^{K} \frac{\Pr[S = 0|Z = k]}{\Pr[S = 1|Z = 1]}$, when $r_1 < 1$, $$\mathrm{E}[Y(1)|U = 1, S(1) = 1] \le \mathrm{E}[Y|Y \ge Q_{Y|Z=1,S=1}(r_1), Z = 1, S = 1].$$ [Corrected statement in full] Under Assumptions 1–3 (Assumption 3 as corrected in P010-T17), with $U$ as in the proof ($U = 1$ if $S(2) = \cdots = S(K) = 1$, else $U = 0$), $\Pr[S(1) = \cdots = S(K) = 1] > 0$, and $Y$ continuous with $\mathrm{E}[|Y|\,|\,Z = 1, S = 1] < \infty$: (i) the conditional distribution of $Y(1)$ given $S(1) = 1$ equals the conditional distribution of $Y$ given $S = 1$ and $Z = 1$, and $\Pr[S(k) = 1] = \Pr[S = 1|Z = k]$ for every $k$; (ii) hence $\sum_{k=2}^{K}\Pr[S(k) = 0]/\Pr[S(1) = 1] = r_1$ and $\mathrm{E}[Y(1)|Y(1) \ge Q_{Y(1)|S(1)=1}(r_1), S(1) = 1] = \mathrm{E}[Y|Y \ge Q_{Y|Z=1,S=1}(r_1), Z = 1, S = 1]$; (iii) when $r_1 < 1$, $\mathrm{E}[Y(1)|S(1) = S(2) = \cdots = S(K) = 1] = \mathrm{E}[Y(1)|U = 1, S(1) = 1] \le \mathrm{E}[Y|Y \ge Q_{Y|Z=1,S=1}(r_1), Z = 1, S = 1]$, which is the upper bound of Proposition 1 for $z = 1$ in the corrected form of P010-T4.

Given continuity of $Y(1)$, then among all possible joint distributions $(Y(1), U)|S(1) = 1$, $\mathrm{E}[Y(1)|U = 1, S(1) = 1]$ is maximized when $U = 1$ for all $Y(1) \ge Q_{Y(1)}(p_{U^0})$. By weak monotonicity of the quantile function, it suffices to maximize $p_{U^0}$ to find a maximum for $\mathrm{E}[Y(1)|U = 1, S(1) = 1]$. We again do not observe the joint distribution $(U, S(1))$. By $\sigma$-additivity, a sharp upper bound is obtained for $\Pr[U = 0]$ is obtained when the regions where $S(2), S(3), \ldots, S(K)$ each equal zero are disjoint, with $$\Pr[U = 0] \le \begin{cases} \sum_{k=2}^{K} \Pr[S(k) = 0] & : \sum_{k=2}^{K} \Pr[S(k) = 0] < 1 \\ 1 & : \sum_{k=2}^{K} \Pr[S(k) = 0] \ge 1. \end{cases}$$ Thus, among all possible joint distributions $(U, S(1))$, $\Pr[U = 0|S(1) = 1] = p_{U^0}$ is maximized when $$p_{U^0} = \begin{cases} \frac{\sum_{k=2}^{K} \Pr[S(k) = 0]}{\Pr[S(1) = 1]} & : \frac{\sum_{k=2}^{K} \Pr[S(k) = 0]}{\Pr[S(1) = 1]} < 1 \\ 1 & : \frac{\sum_{k=2}^{K} \Pr[S(k) = 0]}{\Pr[S(1) = 1]} \ge 1. \end{cases}$$” [$Q_{Y(1)|S(1)=1}$ is used in the proof without a separate definition: the quantile function of the conditional distribution of $Y(1)$ given $S(1) = 1$.
